items.t: put the evidence in order and find patient zero.
Rewind to before the attacker got in. Deploy controls on a budget and replay the real attack.

blocks.small: Stars: stop it early, waste nothing on decoys, keep users happy.

briefing.opening: Just before 5:00 AM. There's a ransom note on an IT system.

act1.title: Rebuild the timeline
act1.short: Put the evidence in the order it happened. Red herrings go to Not related.
act1.help: Drag an evidence card onto the timeline in the order it happened, or onto Not related. You can also tap a card, then use the buttons.
act1.pzHelp: Tap the timeline entry that shows the first successful access.
act1.doneHelp: Six steps from a forgotten VPN profile to a pipeline shutdown.
act1.finding: Patient zero was the legacy VPN profile: one sign-in with a valid password and no second factor. The profile was not intended to be in use and did not show up in penetration tests. From there the attacker reached the IT network, copied data off the share drive and encrypted IT systems. The pipeline was shut down to keep the malware away from the OT network.

hints.1: Before anyone can sign in, they need something. Where does it come from?
hints.2: Which log shows the first time they actually got in?
hints.3: Once inside, where did the VPN session go next?
hints.4: Before encrypting, they took something with them.
hints.6: What did operators do to protect the pipeline?

timeline.text: The attacker obtained the password of an account that could use a legacy VPN profile. How was still under investigation.
timeline.why: It happened outside Colonial's network. A complicated password doesn't help once someone else knows it.

timeline.text: Signed in through a legacy VPN profile that was not intended to be in use. It had single-factor authentication.
timeline.why: One password was enough. Colonial's normal remote access used RSA tokens, but this profile didn't, and it did not show up in penetration tests.

timeline.text: Moved within Colonial's IT systems. The forensic investigation was still retracing exactly how.
timeline.why: A valid VPN session looks like an employee working remotely.

timeline.text: Exfiltrated data off the share drive. The ransom note told Colonial the data had been taken.
timeline.why: Stolen data gives criminals a second lever: pay, or it leaks.

timeline.text: DarkSide ransomware encrypted IT systems. An employee found the ransom note just before 5:00 AM EDT.
timeline.why: By the time the note appeared, the encryption had already run.

timeline.text: To keep the malware from spreading to the OT network, operators shut down all 5,500 miles of pipeline by 6:10 AM. Lines began returning to service on the evening of May 12.
timeline.why: Nobody could yet tell whether the malware had reached OT, so stopping everything was the safe call. Colonial paid the ransom on May 8.

rewind: Now rewind. You're Colonial's security team, before anyone tried that VPN profile. Stop it.

stages.name: Attacker gets a valid VPN password
Sign in via the legacy VPN profile, password only
Copy data off the share drive
Encrypt IT systems, leave ransom note
Pipeline shut down to protect OT
stages.impactNote: Not an attacker action: Colonial's operators shut the pipeline down to keep the malware away from the OT network.

map.note: ATT&CK codes for each stage come from the timeline above, so Act 1 and Act 2 always match.

controls.name: MFA on the VPN gateway (known profiles)
controls.why: Every profile in your inventory now asks for a second factor, including the legacy one you found.
controls.whyScoped: Covered the known profiles only. The legacy profile wasn't in your inventory, so a password alone still worked.
controls.teach: Blount told the Senate that MFA is “absolutely the correct advice.”

controls.name: Audit remote-access (VPN) profiles
controls.why: Found it: a legacy VPN profile that was not intended to be in use, with single-factor authentication.
controls.teach: Blount said it didn't show up in any pen testing. An inventory finds doors like this.

controls.name: Disable the legacy VPN profile
controls.why: The legacy profile no longer existed, so the password opened nothing.
controls.teach: Colonial shut the profile down after the attack.

controls.name: EDR on IT servers and laptops
controls.why: Unusual activity from the VPN session raised an alert early.
controls.teach: EDR watches behaviour, not just known malware.

controls.name: Alert on large outbound transfers
controls.why: A big copy from the share drive to an outside host raised an alert.
controls.teach: Stolen data has to leave through your network. Watch what leaves.

controls.name: Rehearsed incident response plan
controls.why: Trained staff acted at once: the note was reported, the response process started and the FBI was called that morning.
controls.teach: Blount credited Colonial's incident response process and everyone's stop work authority.

controls.name: Offline, tested backups
controls.why: IT systems can come back from backups the ransomware couldn't reach.
controls.teach: Blount said Mandiant told him Colonial had really good backups, and restoring still took days.

controls.name: Segment IT from OT, with monitored crossings
controls.why: The ransomware stayed on the IT side and operators could show OT was separate, so the pipeline kept running.
controls.teach: After the attack Blount said Colonial wants “the best segmentation we can possibly have on our OT side.”

controls.name: Stronger password complexity rules
controls.why: The password was already complicated, “not a ‘Colonial 123’ type password.” Once known, it still worked.

controls.name: Lockout after 5 failed tries
controls.why: The attacker had the right password. Lockout only counts wrong guesses.

controls.name: Geo-block foreign VPN sign-ins
controls.why: A valid password works just as well from a server inside the country.

controls.name: VPN login warning banner
controls.why: A banner only has legal value. Attackers click through it.

controls.name: Disk encryption on file servers
controls.why: It protects a stolen disk. A signed-in session reads the files decrypted.

controls.name: Cyber insurance policy
controls.why: It may pay some costs afterwards. It stops no stage of the attack.

stars.two: stopped at the entry stage (damage NONE). That needs every way in discovered first.
stars.three: ★★ plus at least one detect and one recover control in the build
stars.nextOne: ★: stop the attack at any stage.
stars.nextTwo: ★★: stop it at the entry stage. Find every way in before you lock the door.
stars.nextThree: ★★★: add a detect and a recover layer in case prevention fails.

act2.title: Harden the network
act2.short: Before the break-in. Deploy controls on a budget, then run the real attack against your build.
act2.help: Tap a control to deploy or remove it, or drag it onto a stage in the zone it protects. Each control costs energy and the budget is 8, so you can't buy everything. Not every asset is in your inventory yet: discovery controls find what's missing. Then execute the attack: it replays stage by stage against your build, and the log explains every result.
act2.attemptedNote: Getting hold of a password happens outside your network, so you can't block it there. Defense starts at stage 2, when the password meets the VPN.

prevented.title: Breach prevented
prevented.sub: Attack chain broken at stage {n} of {total}. They never got in.

contained.title: Breach contained
contained.sub: They got into IT, but you stopped them at stage {n} of {total}, before the pipeline.

detected.title: Breach detected
detected.sub: The attack ran its course, but your detection caught it in progress.

succeeded.title: Breach succeeded
succeeded.sub: Like the real incident: IT encrypted, data stolen and the pipeline down for days.

tips.notStopped: The attack ran all the way. Check where it really got in, and whether that profile was in your inventory.
tips.unknownAsset: The attacker entered via an asset not in your inventory. You can't protect what you haven't found.
tips.notEntry: Stopped, but only after they got in. For ★★, stop it at the entry stage.
tips.needLayers: Prevention held. For ★★★, add a detect and a recover layer in case it fails next time.
tips.decoys: {n} decoy(s) cost budget but did nothing against this attack.
tips.friction: High friction: users will push back. Find a lighter build.

always.t: CISA and FBI's DarkSide advisory starts with MFA for remote access to IT and OT networks, and covers IT/OT segmentation and regular offline backups.
